instructional_purpose: Introduces the register-bounded notion of licensed deviation in metrical verse and surveys a six-item taxonomy of such deviations, so that a reader parsing verse tests for a sanctioned licence before declaring a form ungrammatical.

meter and rhyme as the pressure that licenses deviation

the evidence hierarchy that ranked early verse above ordinary prose
restraint as a critical criterion: licences tolerated, not encouraged

linguistic_propositions.proposition: Deviations of this class are permitted only inside metrical verse and carry no permission into prose.
The class of licensed deviations is exhaustively enumerable as exactly six types.
Prose admits no grammatical deviation whatsoever.
These operations alter phonological shape only; the word keeps the syntactic role and case it would have in its prose form.
Adding nunation to a blocked noun supplies the extra syllable the meter requires.
The kasra on the rhyme-final place name in the famous pre-Islamic ode opening is an instance of granting declension to a blocked noun.
Two of the six types are supported here only by hedged, variant-dependent readings introduced with qualifiers such as possibly and in some readings.
Withholding nunation from an ordinarily nunated noun is rarer, disputed, and read by some critics as a sign of weak craft.
The sixth type is often absorbed into pause phenomena rather than counted as a licence.

the departure must map onto one of the recognised types

exceptions: vowel prolongation at the end of a hemistich is treated as ordinary pause practice rather than as a licence
an irregular-looking form may instead be corruption, a transmission variant, or a poet error

contrasts: verse permission vs prose prohibition

common_mistakes.pattern: Using a licensed verse form in prose and defending it as licence.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The permission is bounded to the verse register; outside it the same form is simply incorrect.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Gate the whole rule set on register before any form is evaluated.

common_mistakes.pattern: Reversing the direction of the lengthen/shorten pair.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The two operations are inverses, so naming one for the other inverts the analysis and predicts the wrong prose source form.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Anchor each label to whether the final glottal-stop element is removed or supplied.

common_mistakes.pattern: Assuming every noun of the blocked class carries nunation once it appears in verse.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The override is optional and pressure-triggered, not a blanket property of the verse register.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Require an identifiable metrical or rhyme trigger before diagnosing the override.

common_mistakes.pattern: Labelling every unusual form encountered in verse as a licence.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Irregularity has other sources, including corruption and transmission variance.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Treat licence as a residual diagnosis reached only after the other sources are excluded.

common_mistakes.pattern: Treating licence use as stylistically neutral.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The critical tradition penalised frequent recourse, so a licence-dense reading is evidence of misanalysis or of weak craft, never of normal practice.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Record licence use as marked and countable rather than free.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: An indefinite blocked noun takes fatha in the genitive slot and never carries nunation.
Blocking requires two features, one of which must be name-hood or adjectivehood.
Broken plurals on the ultimate-plural templates are blocked regardless of the singular they derive from.
With the definite article, or as head of a construct, a blocked noun takes kasra in the genitive, and this is ordinary prose grammar rather than a licence.
In verse a poet may supply nunation, or genitive kasra, to a blocked noun when meter or rhyme demands it.
The nasal ending added by nunation supplies the extra syllable the meter needs.
Blocking is caused by phonological heaviness of the noun.
The foundational grammarian expressly conceded a licence to poets on this point, in the terms given here.
The rhyme-final place name in the famous ode opening exhibits this override.
The template-to-example table for ultimate plurals is internally consistent.

common_mistakes.pattern: Adding nunation to a blocked noun in prose and calling it licence.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The override is bounded to verse; in prose the form is an error with no defence available.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Gate the override on register before evaluating the form.

common_mistakes.pattern: Forgetting that a definite or construct-headed blocked noun takes kasra.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The learner either marks correct prose as wrong, or misreads ordinary definiteness-driven kasra as a poetic override.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Run the definiteness test before the override test, since it explains most kasra sightings.

common_mistakes.pattern: Mismatching which two features license the blocking of a given noun.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: A single feature never blocks on the feature-based route, and citing the wrong pair leaves the class assignment unjustified.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Name both features explicitly and check that one of them is primary.

common_mistakes.pattern: Assuming any proper name is blocked.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Name-hood is only a primary feature; without a second feature the name is fully declinable and takes nunation normally.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Require a second feature before assigning the blocked class.

common_mistakes.pattern: Diagnosing the override wherever a blocked noun appears in verse.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Meters frequently accommodate the ordinary blocked form, so the diagnosis needs positive evidence of deviation.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Diagnose only where nunation or kasra appears in a slot that the prose class would not permit.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: A noun ending in a bare final alif cannot carry a visible case marker, so its case is estimated.
A noun whose ending is alif plus glottal stop carries its case marker visibly on the glottal stop.
Either operation changes phonological shape only: case, syntactic role and part of speech are unchanged, though the case marker moves between visible and estimated.
Shortening is broadly accepted while extending is accepted but rarer.
Every listed shortened noun has a corresponding extended poetic variant, and vice versa.
Shortening is the more common of the two because the language contains more extended-ending nouns.
Each operation adds or removes exactly one mora.
A relative-adjective form cited in passing represents a separate licence of the same family.
Both operations are restricted to verse and are errors in prose.

common_mistakes.pattern: Writing a shortened verse form in prose.

common_mistakes.pattern: Skipping the parse because the form looks irregular.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The operation is phonological, so the case and role are still fully determinate and must still be stated.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Parse from the prose source form and record the marker as estimated where the shortened shape blocks a visible one.

common_mistakes.pattern: Reading every such ending as evidence of an applied operation.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Most nouns belong natively to one class, so the default reading is class membership rather than deviation.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Consult the lexicon default before positing any operation.

common_mistakes.pattern: Assuming poets apply these operations freely.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Critical practice penalised licence density, so a reading that finds them everywhere is almost certainly misanalysing ordinary forms.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Treat a high licence count in one passage as a signal to re-check the class assignments.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: Head and complement form one grammatical unit: the head is deprived of nunation and the complement fixes the definiteness of the whole.
In prose, nothing whatsoever may intervene between head and complement.
The classes of material a poet may interpose are the vocative, a negator, an oath, a prepositional phrase and a parenthetical remark.
Interposition is not free even in verse: only sanctioned types are admitted.
The separated strings offered as illustrations are cited attestations.
The flagship cited ode line demonstrates the taught phenomenon.
Documentary and legal prose may stretch the same adjacency norm for precision.
A head noun lacking nunation and semantically incomplete signals an unresolved construct.

common_mistakes.pattern: Interposing material inside a construct in prose.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: In the prose register the sequence is ungrammatical and no licence is available.

common_mistakes.pattern: Reading an apposition as a separated construct.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: In apposition the second noun re-identifies the first rather than completing it, so no genitive dependency exists to recover.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Require a genuine head-complement semantic fit and genitive marking before positing separation.

common_mistakes.pattern: Treating any interruption as sanctioned.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Only catalogued classes of interposer are admitted, so an arbitrary insertion is not licensed even in verse.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Check the interposer against the sanctioned list before accepting the reading.

common_mistakes.pattern: Failing to notice the construct at all and leaving the head unresolved.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The head is left without a complement, so its lack of nunation and its definiteness go unexplained and the line is misparsed.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Whenever a noun lacks nunation and is semantically incomplete, search forward for its complement before closing the parse.

common_mistakes.pattern: Treating documentary or legal phrasing as poetic licence.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The registers differ and so do the conventions and their justifications, so the licence account does not transfer.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Identify the register and apply its own norms rather than importing the verse licence.

proposed_new_units.summary: An adjacency constraint on the construct expressed as a licensing table: required in prose, relaxable in verse for listed interposer classes under a stated motive, plus a recovery procedure for a delayed complement.
proposed_new_units.why_existing_insufficient: u-n03 covers government and u-n10 covers attachment and scope, but neither encodes adjacency as a violable constraint with an enumerated relaxation set, and neither can gate that relaxation on register.

instructional_purpose: Treats verse-level manipulation of verbal valency, both supplying a direct object to a verb whose default frame excludes one and withholding the object of a verb whose frame requires one, and attaches the two grammatical schools' rival accounts of whether valency is inherent or contextual.
concepts_taught: default valency: object-taking vs non-object-taking verbs
the accusative-object substitution test
prepositional complementation as the ordinary route for a non-object-taking verb
supplying a bare accusative object to such a verb in verse
withholding the object of an object-taking verb
rhetorical effects claimed for each device: personification, externalisation, absoluteness

the division of labour between grammatical description and rhetorical explanation

linguistic_propositions.proposition: Verbs divide by whether they license a bare accusative object, testable by substitution.
A non-object-taking verb ordinarily reaches its complement through a preposition.
In verse a poet may give such a verb a bare accusative object.
Withholding the object of an object-taking verb is a poetic licence restricted to verse.
The paired label used here for withholding an object is the established classical term for the phenomenon.
The verb of weeping used throughout is intransitive by nature, so an accusative after it always signals the device.
The Basran position takes valency as fixed and treats verse counterexamples as tolerated necessity; the Kufan position takes valency as contextual and treats them as proof that it is not fixed.
Both schools agree the devices are permitted in verse and disagree only on what that permission implies for the rule.
The attribution of this account to a named classical dispute compendium is carried by a lesson-composed passage in classical style.
Attributing an action to an entity that cannot literally perform it is intellectual metaphor.
The tabulated rhetorical effects follow from the devices.
The illustrative verse lines given for both devices are cited attestations.

recognition_criteria: an accusative noun governed directly by a verb whose lexical frame does not license one, with no preposition mediating
an object-taking verb with no object present where the frame requires one
the missing object is not recoverable from the immediate context, so the gap is doing rhetorical work
the grammatical subject is a non-agentive entity, signalling figurative attribution
verse register

check the context for an unexpected accusative object, or for an unexpected absence of one
classify the device by which of the two configurations is found
distinguish a derived causative form, which changes the verb's pattern, from a valency shift that leaves the pattern intact
for a missing object, decide whether it is contextually recoverable, which is ordinary usage, or withheld for effect
state the rhetorical effect and the reason the poet preferred it to ordinary phrasing
conditions: verse register for the licensed reading
the verb's default frame must be established independently before any deviation is claimed
for object withholding, the absence of a recoverable antecedent is what makes the reading rhetorical rather than ordinary
exceptions: object omission under recoverability is ordinary usage in prose and needs no licence at all
a derived causative form takes an object by derivation, not by licence
a verb attested with an object in ordinary classical usage is not shifted merely because an object appears
contrasts: supplying an object vs withholding one

common_mistakes.pattern: Confusing a valency shift with a derived causative form.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The causative changes the verb's pattern and licenses the object by derivation, whereas the poetic shift leaves the pattern untouched.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Inspect the verb's form before classifying: a pattern change rules out the licence reading.

common_mistakes.pattern: Treating every omitted object as a poetic device.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Omission under recoverability is ordinary usage in any register, so the device claim needs the additional evidence that no antecedent is recoverable.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Test recoverability first and diagnose the device only where the gap is doing rhetorical work.

common_mistakes.pattern: Marking a licensed accusative object as an error when parsing verse.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The construction is a recognised permission in the verse register, so flagging it as ungrammatical misreads the text.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Apply the register gate before assigning any error.

common_mistakes.pattern: Naming the device and stopping there.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The classification is only half the analysis; the reason the poet deviated is what the deviation was for.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Pair every device label with the image or emphasis it produces.

common_mistakes.pattern: Using either device in prose.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The permission is bounded to verse, and outside it the supplied object in particular is simply ungrammatical.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Gate on register, and note that the two devices are not equally register-bound, since recoverable omission is ordinary prose.

tutor_drill_relevance: high + valency discrimination and device classification are cleanly drillable and the closing classification grid is a genuine drill, though the phrases used are constructed rather than cited

corpus_pvn_relevance: verb-side: verb entries need a valency frame field plus a flag for verbs attested with an object outside their nominal frame, and a separate marker for verse-only shifted uses; particle and noun yield is negligible
required_evidence: per occurrence: the verb's default frame with lexicographic support, the register, the presence or absence of a preposition, a recoverability judgement for any missing object, and a cited line, since every illustration in this lesson is constructed
uncertainty_flags: the two devices are presented as equally verse-restricted, but the lesson itself states that object omission under recoverability is ordinary prose, so the register scoping of the second device is inconsistent and must not be projected as a poetry-only rule

the verb used throughout as the type case is attested with a direct object in ordinary classical usage in a mourning sense, which weakens the diagnostic
the classification of the personifying example under intellectual metaphor competes with a reading as implicit simile, and the schools' positions are reported without primary citation

proposed_new_units.summary: A licensing table over verbal valency: default frame, the conditions under which a bare accusative object is admitted outside that frame, the conditions separating recoverable omission from rhetorical withholding, and the school attribution attached to each reading.
proposed_new_units.why_existing_insufficient: u-n03 and u-n04 cover government and accusative complements as they stand, and u-n11 holds rival analyses, but none of them represents a verb frame as a defeasible licensing condition with register and recoverability as the defeaters.

new_capability_required: an elision-recoverability check: distinguishing an object omitted because it is recoverable from one withheld for effect requires discourse-level evidence that no current capability family supplies
